homeostasis:
Your body holds dozens of variables inside narrow ranges: core temperature, blood pressure, blood glucose, the pH and salt content of your blood. Each one is held the same way. A sensory receptor detects the variable, a control center compares it with a set point, and effectors push it back. Because the correction opposes the change, this is negative feedback, and it is how almost all regulation works.

Watch for it everywhere. When you stand up quickly and blood pools in your legs, pressure sensors in your arteries fire less, your brainstem raises heart rate and tightens arterioles, and your blood pressure recovers within seconds. The same loop, with different parts, runs your thermostat, your breathing and your kidneys. Positive feedback, which amplifies a change, is rare and always has an end point, such as childbirth or a clot sealing a wound.
gradients:
Almost everything that moves in your body moves down a gradient: from high to low pressure, concentration, voltage or temperature. How fast it moves follows one rule. Flow equals the driving difference divided by the resistance. Double the difference and flow doubles; double the resistance and flow halves.

The rule is the same whether the thing moving is blood, air, water, ions or heat. Blood flows from the aorta toward the veins because pressure falls along the way, and narrowing an arteriole cuts flow sharply because resistance rises steeply as a tube gets narrower. Sodium rushes into a neuron because both its concentration and the voltage push it in. When you meet a new process, ask: what is the gradient, and what sets the resistance?
communication:
Trillions of cells act as one body because they signal to each other. Some signals are electrical, spreading along a nerve or through the gap junctions that link heart muscle cells. Most are chemical: a cell releases a messenger, and it acts on any cell that carries a matching receptor protein, whether that cell is next door or across the body.

The receptor protein, not the messenger, decides what happens. The same messenger can speed one tissue and slow another because the two carry different receptor proteins. That is why one nerve signal can raise your heart rate and narrow your skin's blood vessels at the same time, and why a drug that blocks one kind of receptor protein can have such a precise effect.
structure-function:
What a structure does follows from how it is built, at every level. A capillary wall is a single thin layer of cells, so gases cross it in a fraction of a second. The left ventricle has a wall about three times thicker than the right because it pumps against much higher pressure. A heart valve's flaps are tethered by cords so they close under pressure instead of flipping inside out.

Use this in both directions. Given a structure, predict what it can do: a thick, muscular wall squeezes; a thin, leaky one exchanges. Given a job, predict the structure: a surface built for absorption will be folded to add area. It is the fastest way to remember anatomy, because each detail has a reason.
mass-balance:
The amount of any substance in your body changes only by what comes in, what goes out, what is made and what is used up. If intake and output match, the amount stays steady. If you take in more salt than you excrete, total body sodium rises until something changes.

This simple bookkeeping explains a great deal. Blood volume falls after bleeding because output jumped; it recovers as your kidneys cut output and thirst raises intake. When a lab value is abnormal, mass balance tells you where to look: something is coming in too fast, leaving too slowly, being made or being used.
energy:
Every cell runs on ATP. Cells break down food molecules and capture part of the released energy by making ATP; they spend ATP to pump ions against their gradients, to contract, and to build large molecules. Most ATP is made in mitochondria, which need a steady supply of oxygen.

That is why tissues with a high, unstoppable demand are the most fragile when blood flow fails. Heart muscle beats every second of your life and relies almost entirely on oxygen, so a blocked coronary artery injures it within minutes. When you meet any active process, ask where its ATP comes from and what happens when the supply stops.
compartments:
Membranes divide your body into compartments with different contents: the fluid inside cells, the fluid around them, and the blood plasma. The plasma membrane keeps potassium high inside a cell and sodium high outside; the capillary wall keeps most plasma proteins in the blood.

Life depends on these differences, and on controlling what crosses between compartments. Water follows solute across membranes, so a change in one compartment's salt concentration moves water in or out of cells. When fluid collects in the wrong compartment, as in swollen ankles, ask which barrier or which force changed.
interdependence:
No organ system works alone. Your heart pumps, but your kidneys set how much blood it has to pump, your nervous system sets its rate, and your lungs load the blood it carries with oxygen. A change in one system is sensed and answered by others.

This is why a single problem spreads. After heavy bleeding, the heart speeds up, the blood vessels tighten, the kidneys hold on to water and the thirst center pushes you to drink, all to protect blood pressure. When you study a system, ask what it depends on and what depends on it.
